articles.title: Brickbat: Pick Up the Phone
articles.content:
德州奥德萨市前警官乔迪·贝尔（Jody Baer）因滥用职务信息面临两项重罪指控。调查人员表示，他利用工作中获取的电话号码，向两名曾被他逮捕的女性发送带有个人性质和不当性暗示的短信。

根据控状，贝尔于8月5日首次联系其中一名女性，很快便开始发送带有性暗示的信息。另一起事件则始于8月22日，他对另一名女性使用了“美丽”和“性感”等形容词，调查人员还发现他多次驾驶标有警车从该女士家门前经过，并通过短信询问她是否在家。两名女性均向调查人员表示，她们曾将未公开的电话号码提供给贝尔，因为他是警方人员。

贝尔在逮捕当天清晨辞职，并在审讯中承认利用逮捕时获取的电话号码主动联系这两名女性，称自己感到孤独。调查人员表示，他还承认发送了一些不当信息，包括向其中一名女性发送性暗示内容及照片。

该事件最初由《理性杂志》报道，标题为“砖块：接电话”。
articles.summary:
Jody Baer, a former police officer in Odessa, Texas, faces two felony counts of misuse of official information. Investigators say he used phone numbers obtained through his job to send personal and sexually inappropriate text messages to two women he had arrested. According to an affidavit, Baer first contacted one woman on August 5, and his messages soon became sexual in nature. He allegedly contacted another woman starting on August 22, calling her "beautiful" and "sexy"; investigators also say he drove his marked patrol vehicle past her home several times and asked by text if she was there. Both women told investigators they had given Baer their phone numbers, which were not publicly available, because he was a police officer. Baer acknowledged obtaining their numbers during their arrests and contacting them afterward, explaining that he was lonely. Investigators say he also admitted that some of the messages were inappropriate, including sending a sexual message and photograph to one of the women. Baer resigned the morning of his arrest.

The post Brickbat: Pick Up the Phone appeared first on Reason Magazine.

articles.title: Because KBJ Denied Administrative Stay in Third-Country Removal Case, The Application Should Be Referred To The Full Court Now
articles.content:
美国政府再次申请最高法院紧急干预第三国遣返案：关键争议焦点

联邦检察总长在《美国诉D.V.D.》一案中提出的紧急申请，再次将美国移民政策中"第三国遣返"问题推向风暴中心。这是政府第三次就此类案件向最高法院求助，前两次均获准。检方指出，下级法院最新裁决仍基于同样的法律误区，且新增的论据更显薄弱。随着移民危机持续升温，此案考验着最高法院维护行政权的决心。

检方强调，仅昨晚23:36，第一巡回上诉法院不经听证便突然撤销了对下级法院判决的暂缓执行令。这一突发变故对移民局的日常遣返操作造成严重冲击，包括取消多架遣返航班，涉及70名有犯罪记录的外籍人士（含重罪犯），并导致与三个接收国的外交协调重启。政府担忧，若不能迅速恢复遣返权，将进一步积累安全风险。

此案背景可追溯至2024年修订的移民法，授权政府将部分外籍人士遣返至第三国。检方援引2025年"特朗普诉博伊尔案"，认为最高法院此前暂缓执行令的判断逻辑仍适用本案。然而，第一巡回上诉法院法官德克·哈斯基尔此前已表示，将暂缓执行令延续至2026年5月15日。

检方在申请中特别强调，若巡回法官拒绝立即行政暂缓令，请求将此事提交全体大法官审议。这一策略意在加速审查进程，避免拖延造成更大损失。法学观察家认为，此举反映了政府对第三国遣返政策合法性的坚定立场。

而大法官杰克逊的拒绝行政暂缓令的决定，为该案增加了新变数。从程序角度分析，杰克逊仅允许被申请人4天时间回应，与此前大法官卡瓦诺要求密苏里州14小时内回应的案例形成鲜明对比。这一差异可能暗示着大法官间对移民政策干预时效性的不同认知。
articles.summary:
I may have to eat crow on the lightning docket (no order in the Missouri case), but things are brewing with the third-country removal case. The Solicitor General's emergency application in United States v. D.V.D. lays out the issue neatly:

This is the third time the government has been forced to seek emergency relief from the district court's orders in this case about "third-country removals"—an essential tool to remove certain aliens, including some of the worst criminal aliens. This Court granted relief on both previous occasions. The latest order rests on the same fundamentally flawed legal premises as the previous rulings, and the nominal new grounds that the lower courts added to try to buttress those prior decisions are even weaker than those that failed to sustain the originals. Meanwhile, the equities that supported this Court's intervention (twice) have, if anything, only grown stronger in favor of the government's continued enforcement of the challenged policy. A stay is thus once again warranted. Cf. Trump v. Boyle, 145 S. Ct. 2653, 2654 (2025) ("Although our interim orders are not conclusive as to the merits, they inform how a court should exercise its equitable discretion in like cases."). "Although the posture of the case has changed, the parties' legal arguments and relative harms generally have not. The same result that [this Court] reached in [June 2025] is appropriate here." Noem v. National TPS Alliance, 146 S. Ct. 23, 24 (2025).

An immediate administrative stay is particularly critical. The First Circuit had previously stayed this latest order pending appeal; the government thus has been conducting third-country removals under the challenged policy for the last 15 months. But at 11:36 p.m. last night—without even allowing the government to respond to respondents' motion (itself filed at 8:20 p.m.)—the First Circuit abruptly dissolved the stay. The unexpected springing-back of district court's order has, this Office is informed, created substantial logistical problems with ongoing removal operations— including the cancellation of flights—and led to added expense, potential diplomatic issues, and the inability to remove dangerous criminals. For example, DHS informs us that it has already canceled a flight to three separate countries carrying 70 aliens with criminal convictions (including aggravated assault and serious drug offenses), and that the cancellation has required a new round of diplomatic engagement with each of the three countries. Those disruptions will only get worse. To halt that chaos, an immediate administrative stay should be entered while the Court considers this application. In light of the ongoing disruption caused by the First Circuit as well as the prior stays granted by the full Court, if the Circuit Justice enters a briefing schedule without also entering an immediate administrative stay, the government respect fully requests that its request for the immediate administrative stay be referred to the full Court. Cf. Rollins v. Rhode Island State Council of Churches, 146 S. Ct. 402 (2025) (No. 25A539); A.A.R.P. v. Trump, 145 S. Ct. 1034 (2025) (No. 24A1007).

Circuit Justice Jackson has denied an administrative stay, and granted a four-day response time. That is leisurely compared to the 14 hours Justice Kavanaugh gave Missouri to respond.

I think now the case is in fact referred to the full Court. Let's see whether there are five votes for an administrative stay. I think Justice Jackson tried to call her colleagues' bluff.

My SCOTUSBlog post on empowering the majority offered a similar remedy:

It is not clear how many votes are needed to take a case away from a circuit justice. Here, I propose a clear rule: the Refer-6. Six justices, at any point, can vote to refer any pending matter to the full court. At the latest, the Refer-6 can be invoked after the briefing is completed. The Refer-6 can also be invoked to establish a briefing schedule. Or the Refer-6 can be invoked as soon as an application is filed in order to enter an administrative stay.

Realistically, the Refer-6 can be discussed even before an emergency application is filed. Usually, the clerk of the Supreme Court is given a heads-up that an emergency application is on its way. The Refer-6 can follow a Conference-3. At that point, the justices can informally establish a game plan, given how the case has proceeded through the lower courts. If six justices decide this matter belongs before the full court, the referral can happen right away. Of course, the circuit justice can dissent from the order being referred to the full court. But the circuit justice cannot stop the referral.

Some of my proposals were designed to promote collegiality. The Refer-6 would have just the opposite effect. It would signal that the court did not want a particular circuit justice to have power over a matter. But I suspect this Rubicon was already crossed in the Rhode Island case. Jackson perhaps tried to do too much in her capacity as circuit justice, and her colleagues apparently countermanded her.

Justice Jackson makes the case for unilateral SCOTUS reform.

Update: Today Justice Jackson gave a speech at the University of District of Columbia. And this evening, Chief Justice Roberts, and Justices Barrett and Kavanaugh were at the White House State Dinner. (I wonder if the Chief was given a tour of the new construction he tried to stop.) Query if the Justices somehow had an informal conference about the administrative stay before Jackson denied it.

The post Because KBJ Denied Administrative Stay in Third-Country Removal Case, The Application Should Be Referred To The Full Court Now appeared first on Reason Magazine.

articles.title: Texas Wants Free Speech on Campus—With Exceptions
articles.content:
Gregorio Olivares Gutierrez was an editor of The Mercury, a student newspaper at the University of Texas at Dallas, before he was placed on a two-year deferred suspension after his school deemed that his editorial decisions constituted "discriminatory harassment."
This all started when UT Dallas Hillel president Jade Steinberg sent The Mercury a letter about campus antisemitism and the Israel-Palestine conflict. Gutierrez thought the letter lacked credible sources, so he added a disclaimer to its publication stating that the letter "does not meet the journalistic standards of The Mercury" and should be treated as opinion rather than news. A day after the piece went live, Steinberg complained, leading to Gutierrez's suspension. Gutierrez filed a lawsuit last week, alleging that the school violated his First Amendment rights.
Gutierrez's case is one of many free speech controversies at Texas universities. Texas schools received an average grade of F in the annual college free speech rankings recently published by the Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression (FIRE). The report cites 25 free speech controversies across the state's universities, and 42 percent of students claim to have self-censored at least once a month.
The failing grades are a stark contrast to the state government's recent attempt to support free speech on campus in the wake of conservative activist Charlie Kirk's assassination.
Last year, Texas House Speaker Dustin Burrows (R–Lubbock) and Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick created the House and Senate Select Committees on Civil Discourse & Freedom of Speech in Higher Education. The committee was created in Kirk's honor, just two days after his death, to study bias, discourse, and free speech at universities. In the committee's announcement, Patrick said, "The attack on Charlie was an attack on the First Amendment. Those who cheered his murder are also cheering for the death of America. We cannot tolerate either at our institutions of higher learning."
Yet FIRE noted a slew of free speech controversies over the last couple of years. Among them: Devion Canty Jr. was forced to withdraw from Texas State University after a video of him mocking Kirk went viral enough to cause Gov. Greg Abbott and Rudy Giuliani to call for his expulsion. English department lecturer Melissa McCoul was fired from Texas A&M after a video of her dispute with a student over her teaching "illegal" gender identity material went viral; two of her superiors went down with her because they approved the course. Brooklyn-based street artist Victor Quiñonez had his exhibition shut down by the University of North Texas after an anonymous tip about anti-ICE artwork. Khalid el-Hakim was invited to bring his Black History 101 Mobile Museum to Texas State University—until the school canceled his event by email, citing "Senate Bill 17 (88R), the climate of our State, and certain topics covered as part of the museum."
Texas A&M was penalized by FIRE's rankings for the school's ban on drag shows, which FIRE is now challenging in court. In February 2025, the board of regents voted unanimously to implement the policy, stating that it was "inconsistent with the System's mission and core values." As a result, "Draggieland," the annual drag pageant organized by students, was canceled.
A federal judge blocked Texas A&M's ban in March 2025, allowing the event to proceed. The university system appealed, and the full Fifth Circuit heard arguments on Wednesday, September 23, along with a separate challenge to West Texas A&M's drag show ban.
Texas's principal deputy solicitor general, William "Billy" Cole, argued that the ban targets conduct, not viewpoint and that drag performances could discriminate against women. J.T. Morris, FIRE's supervising senior attorney, argued that the First Amendment has a "mandate for viewpoint neutrality," and rules targeting expression because it is deemed "demeaning" give administrators too much discretion. The court is yet to rule.
Morris tells Reason, "We remain hopeful that the court will uphold the Constitution's staunch protections against viewpoint discrimination and prior restraints that are essential to maintaining public universities as beacons for free expression."
Free speech protections matter most when it comes to speech that is unpopular or offensive. Whether it's a Kirk-related event at the University of California, Berkeley or a drag show at Texas A&M, the same First Amendment protections should apply.
The post Texas Wants Free Speech on Campus—With Exceptions appeared first on Reason Magazine.
